title: Litigation responsibility: Sanctions follow conduct and authority
desc: Documents citation failures across drafting chains, with culpability, correction and procedural context determining consequences.

kps.k: The central proposition is continuing human accountability: AI may assist litigation, but it cannot assume responsibility for accurate submissions.
kps.d: Mata distinguishes permissible, reliable AI assistance from lawyers’ existing responsibility for filings. Noland and Wadsworth require lawyers to read underlying authorities and check that they support the propositions advanced; plausible citations and excerpts do not suffice. Verification must cover existence, quotations, holdings, factual assertions and current legal status, not merely formatting. Fletcher rejects ignorance of AI risks as an excuse while acknowledging careful use can help legal practice.

qs.q: Technological advances are commonplace and there is  nothing inherently improper about using a reliable artificial intelligence tool for assistance.

kps.k: The evidence documents failures of citation integrity, not a general measure of AI reliability or legal reasoning ability.
kps.d: Noland reports pervasive fabricated quotations alongside irrelevant and nonexistent cases. Other incidents involve invented transcript quotations and distorted genuine authorities. These defects differ from ordinary typographical mistakes and from reasonable disagreement about law. A View of How Language Models Will Transform Law cites benchmark results separating reasoning performance from citation accuracy; Whiting similarly accepts that genuine law might have supported reversal while treating fabricated citations as independently sanctionable. Suspicious citations do not themselves establish AI provenance: Ko reserves judgment, and Cassata grounds responsibility in nonverification regardless of how counsel obtained the material.

qs.q: What sets this appeal apart—and the reason we have  elected to publish this opinion—is that nearly all of the legal  quotations in plaintiff’s opening brief, and many of the quotations  in plaintiff’s reply brief, are fabricated.

kps.k: Responsibility extends through the drafting and supervision chain, including lawyers who did not personally use AI.
kps.d: Johnson holds individual attorneys responsible for unchecked motions, including two unaware that AI supplied the citations, while separately finding no equivalent firm culpability. Accounts of Smith distinguish stylistic proofreading from substantive citation review. Kohls suggests that reasonable inquiry may require asking witnesses whether they used AI and how they checked it; it does not announce an unconditional duty to interrogate every witness about AI. Together, these materials support review procedures covering associates, nonlawyer staff, co-counsel and expert submissions rather than reliance on a firm policy or another contributor’s assurances alone.

kps.k: Sanctions depend on the governing authority, culpability and procedural context; fabrication does not produce one automatic penalty.
kps.d: HoosierVac rejects good faith as a defense to Rule 11 sanctions, whereas the reported Cohen decision declines sanctions because it finds no bad faith. Lacey requires circumstance-specific analysis and describes recklessness plus an additional factor as potentially tantamount to bad faith. Johnson invokes inherent powers because Rule 11 does not govern the discovery motions and leaves Alabama’s knowing-misstatement rule unresolved. Whiting invokes inherent authority to supplement Rule 38’s narrower remedies. These distinctions preclude treating negligence, bad faith, a show-cause order, disciplinary referral and final discipline as interchangeable.

kps.k: Candor and correction after discovery materially affect courts’ assessments, but remediation does not erase the original harm.
kps.d: Mata faults counsel for defending fabricated authorities after judicial warnings; accounts of Lacey and Crabill describe incomplete correction, nondisclosure or misleading explanations. By contrast, the Ayinde/Al-Haroun survey reports voluntary disclosure and willingness to withdraw citations as relevant to Cohen’s absence of bad faith. Cassata nevertheless rejects the assumption that sincere apologies or replacement authorities necessarily avoid sanctions. The practical implication is to investigate the entire affected submission and correct the record promptly, rather than patch only the errors an opponent or judge identifies.

kps.k: The policy disagreement concerns AI-specific restrictions versus technology-neutral accuracy duties.
kps.d: Judge Starr’s requirements, reproduced in ethics opinions, mandate certification of nonuse or human checking; materials expressly attributed to Judge Kang add disclosure and recordkeeping. These are court-specific measures, not universal professional rules. Park says existing duties already give licensed counsel adequate notice. Browning accepts criticism that special orders duplicate Rule 11, while a Fifth Circuit commenter favors checking all research and predicts difficulty identifying AI embedded in opaque tools. Lawyering in the Age of Artificial Intelligence opposes aggressive restrictions, although the supplied excerpt does not provide the results underlying that assessment. The supplied Fifth Circuit extracts establish a proposal, not its ultimate disposition.

qs.q: Counsel shall maintain records sufficient to identify, if requested by the Court, those portions of the text of a pleading, brief, or document submitted to the Court which was created or drafted by an AI tool.
qs.a: Mandatory Certification Regarding Generative Artificial Intelligence (Judge Brantley Starr, N.D. Tex., standing order) · Regulators & courts · 2023

qs.q: Indeed, several courts have recently proposed or enacted local rules or orders specifically addressing the use of artificial intelligence tools before the court.[3](#footnote_3) But such a rule is not necessary to inform a licensed attorney, who is a member of the bar of this Court, that she must ensure that her submissions to the Court are accurate.
qs.a: Park v. Kim — Second Circuit opinion referring counsel to the Grievance Panel for a ChatGPT-fabricated citation · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: Self-represented litigants face the same accuracy obligations but unequal capacity to meet them.
kps.d: Al-Hamim rejects ignorance of hallucinations as an exemption from procedural compliance. Kruse acknowledges pro se difficulties but bases dismissal on substantial briefing-rule violations, not AI use alone. Other reports describe warnings or leniency rather than immediate penalties. Who Checks the Citations? emphasizes limited database access, awareness and checking capacity among users who may benefit from cheaper assistance. The resulting access-to-justice tension is substantive: unchecked output can displace stronger arguments and jeopardize a hearing, while these excerpts do not demonstrate that AI assistance generally closes—or widens—the justice gap.

kps.k: Courts seek deterrence and institutional protection, while critics question whether escalating sanctions address the underlying verification burden.
kps.d: The decisions describe wasted opposing-party resources, judicial delay, lost client arguments and potential damage to public trust. Remedies range from warnings and replacement briefs to fines, costs, education, disqualification and regulatory referral. Johnson considers fines and embarrassment insufficient; HoosierVac and Cassata emphasize proportionality and restraint. Who Checks the Citations? argues that sanctions remain reactive and uneven and investigates automated checking through a synthetic, court-informed benchmark, without supplying detection-performance results. Reported growth in documented incidents does not measure model error rates or prove deterrence failure. The malpractice-insurance commentary further infers a future claims pipeline from incidents, not paid-claims evidence.

qs.q: The opposing party expends resources identifying and exposing the fabrication; the court spends time reviewing materials, holding hearings, deliberating about sanctions, and explaining its ruling; the substance of the case is delayed; and public confidence about the trustworthiness of legal proceedings may be diminished.
qs.a: Cassata v. Michael Macrina Architect, P.C. — AI sanctions decision, Suffolk County · Regulators & courts · 2026

vlens.an: The curated academia-and-research sources collectively accept the principal proposition that responsibility for litigation submissions remains with human lawyers and litigants, including where AI use occurs elsewhere in the drafting or supervision chain. Their common reasons are existing reasonable-inquiry and accuracy duties, documented sanctions and procedural consequences for fabricated authorities, and the aggravating effect of failing to disclose, withdraw or correct defective material. They materially develop the synthesis by distinguishing citation integrity from legal-reasoning quality; expanding the taxonomy beyond nonexistent cases to false quotations, pincites and misrepresentations; documenting varied, context-dependent judicial responses; and identifying structural verification burdens, especially for self-represented litigants. Some research responds constructively through automated-verification benchmarks rather than relying on sanctions alone. Material variation concerns policy rather than core accountability: some sources favour or report AI-specific certification and review safeguards, while others regard aggressive AI-specific restrictions as duplicative or misguided because technology-neutral duties already govern accuracy. One source is too fragmentary to establish an authorial position, and several excerpts report courts or third parties rather than advancing independent recommendations. These curated materials should not be treated as representative of academia and research generally.

vlens.an: This curated set of market-analyst, consultancy and press sources accepts the cluster’s principal proposition that humans remain accountable for the accuracy of AI-assisted litigation submissions, and materially develops it in several directions. The common reasoning is that responsibility attaches to the lawyer who signs or files the document; assurances from clerks or other contributors do not replace personal verification; and fabricated authority can cause sanctions, dismissal, disciplinary referral and other procedural consequences. The sources also extend the proposition to self-represented litigants and prospective malpractice-insurance exposure. Material internal variation concerns emphasis rather than disagreement: one compilation stresses signature-based certification and circumstance-sensitive sanction calibration; press reports focus on nondelegable supervision, verification and the limited checking capacity of self-represented litigants; and the insurance commentary infers a future claims pipeline and disproportionate small-firm exposure from documented sanctions incidents, while providing no paid-claims evidence. The Maryland report additionally covers possible rule changes but reports rather than endorses them. These sources should not be treated as representative of the wider professional group, and their number does not indicate prevalence.

vlens.an:
The curated regulators, courts and professional-body sources strongly support the proposition that AI assistance does not displace human responsibility for litigation submissions and that consequences depend on conduct and governing authority. Their common reasoning is that existing duties of reasonable inquiry, accuracy, candor and supervision attach to the lawyer or litigant presenting the material, regardless of whether an AI system, colleague, staff member, witness or another source produced it. Verification must be substantive—covering the existence, meaning and current status of authorities and the accuracy of quotations, facts and arguments—not merely a formatting or plausibility check. These sources also commonly distinguish acceptable, careful AI assistance from unchecked reliance and treat post-discovery candor, comprehensive correction and acceptance of responsibility as material to culpability and remedy.

Material internal variation concerns implementation rather than the core duty. Some courts impose AI-specific certification, disclosure or recordkeeping requirements; others regard existing technology-neutral rules as sufficient and warn that AI-specific rules may duplicate established duties or be impractical where AI is embedded in opaque tools. Sanctions approaches also vary with procedural authority and culpability: Rule 11, appellate rules, inherent powers and disciplinary procedures have different thresholds and remedies; negligence, recklessness, bad faith, show-cause proceedings, referrals and final discipline are therefore not interchangeable. Some decisions emphasize proportionate and restrained deterrence, while others conclude that monetary sanctions alone are inadequate. The sources likewise apply accuracy duties to self-represented litigants while showing variation between warnings, leniency and dismissal, and several preserve uncertainty about AI provenance where suspect citations alone do not prove hallucination. These differences refine the proposition but do not undermine its central direction.

elens.an: The curated 2023–2024 sources strongly support the cluster’s principal proposition. Across judicial decisions, ethics opinions, task-force guidance and commentary, the common ground is that generative AI may assist litigation work but does not displace the responsibility of lawyers—or, procedurally, self-represented litigants—to verify submissions. The recurring evidence concerns fabricated or distorted authorities, inadequate reasonable inquiry, and failures of candor or correction, rather than a general measurement of AI reliability or legal reasoning ability. The sources also support the proposition that consequences depend on governing authority and conduct: outcomes range from warnings, rejection of arguments and disciplinary referral to fines or suspension, while serious negligence did not invariably lead to sanctions absent the required bad faith. Material variation concerns policy rather than basic accountability. Some judges imposed AI-specific certification, disclosure or recordkeeping requirements; others and several commentators argued that existing, technology-neutral duties such as Rule 11 already provide adequate notice and that AI-specific restrictions may be duplicative or impractical. Some sources further extend verification to fee applications, controlling contrary precedent and records identifying AI-drafted text. Treatment of self-represented litigants likewise varies between warnings, leniency and dismissal based on substantial procedural violations, but the sources do not treat self-representation or ignorance of hallucination risks as an exemption. This assessment describes only the supplied curated sources and does not establish how prevalent these positions were among courts, lawyers or professional bodies generally.

elens.an: The curated 2025 sources strongly support the cluster’s principal proposition that AI assistance does not displace human responsibility for accurate litigation submissions and that consequences depend on conduct and governing authority. Courts and commentary repeatedly ground verification in existing, technology-neutral professional and procedural duties: lawyers must inspect underlying authorities, responsibility can extend through drafting, signature, supervision and expert-witness chains, and fabricated citations remain serious even where the filing lawyer did not personally operate the AI. The common reasons are protection of citation integrity, judicial trust, opposing-party and court resources, clients’ authentic arguments and public confidence. Material variation concerns consequences rather than the core duty. Some decisions treat good faith as insufficient under Rule 11, while others require bad faith or equivalent recklessness under inherent powers; correction, candor and apology may mitigate the response but do not erase harm. Remedies range from warnings and withdrawal to costs, monetary sanctions, disqualification and regulatory referral. Some sources also preserve uncertainty about whether suspicious citations were AI-generated, distinguish citation incidents from measured model reliability, or highlight self-represented litigants’ limited verification capacity. One footnote-only source is insufficient to establish an authorial position, and access-to-justice aspirations for reliable AI remain compatible with the proposition but are not evidence that AI has closed the justice gap. These internal differences refine rather than undermine the proposition.

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the principal proposition that responsibility remains with the human filer and materially develop it with newer case-level, doctrinal and operational detail. Courts and commentaries commonly ground accountability in the lawyer’s signature, personal verification duty, supervision of associates and nonlawyer staff, and responsibility across co-counsel relationships—not in proof that AI generated the defect. They also reinforce that citation-integrity failures include fabricated cases, false quotations, distorted authorities and factual misrepresentations, while distinguishing those defects from ordinary drafting mistakes and from whether the underlying claim or appeal had legitimate legal support. Material variation concerns consequences and proposed responses: courts apply different governing powers and calibrate outcomes from warnings or replacement briefs to monetary sanctions, costs, disqualification and disciplinary referral, with culpability, candor, correction, procedural posture and prior conduct affecting the result. Some sources extend beyond adjudication by identifying unequal verification capacity among self-represented litigants, developing an automated citation-checking benchmark, or predicting malpractice-insurance exposure. Those extensions do not displace human accountability: they argue that sanctions alone may not solve structural verification burdens and, in the insurance source, rest on documented incidents rather than paid-claims evidence. Because the corpus is curated, this alignment should not be treated as evidence of prevalence across courts, researchers or practitioners generally.
